idiom_name: SQLite spool table (journal_mode=WAL, synchronous=FULL) + drain thread
implementation_notes: Use SQLite as the embedded local store: PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL switches to the write-ahead log and PRAGMA synchronous=FULL makes each commit sync the WAL, so a committed INSERT is the accept point (with the usual WAL setting NORMAL, committed transactions survive process crashes but not power loss). A worker thread - std::jthread, or a loop parked on a std::condition_variable - reads the oldest rows, delivers them and deletes a row only after the peer acknowledged; the sender and the drainer share one connection behind a std::mutex or use separate connections, in which case SQLITE_BUSY/SQLITE_LOCKED must be handled as backpressure rather than as a fatal error. A file-based spool using std::filesystem::rename is the alternative when SQLite must not be linked; the hand-written structure is justified whenever the payload must survive the process and no messaging runtime is available.
pitfalls: synchronous=NORMAL (the usual WAL recommendation) commits without syncing the WAL, so a power loss rolls back messages the sender already accepted.
SQLITE_BUSY / SQLITE_LOCKED from a second writer connection must be retried with a delay instead of failing the accept path.
Deleting the row before the acknowledgement, or deleting by payload instead of by primary key, drops messages the peer never processed.
The drain thread must be joined before the sqlite3 handle is closed; a detached thread touching a closed handle crashes the process.

variants.name: Boost.Asio forwarder with a file spool and timer-driven backoff
variants.idiom_name: io_context steady_timer retry chain over a spool directory
variants.implementation_notes: When no embedded database is available the forwarder becomes an Asio completion chain: after each delivery attempt a steady_timer re-arms with exponential backoff while the peer is unreachable, and the same io_context can carry the delivery socket, so no dedicated drain thread is needed. The spool itself stays one file per message written with fsync + rename; the timer handler owns the retry state, which makes the backoff policy explicit instead of a sleep inside a loop. Choose it in embedded or dependency-averse builds, or where the sender already runs an Asio-based network stack.
pitfalls: The timer must outlive async_wait; a local steady_timer that goes out of scope cancels the retry chain silently.
Blocking file I/O or a blocking send inside an io_context handler stalls the whole executor - post it to a thread pool instead.
Unbounded doubling of the delay can strand messages forever once the peer returns; cap the backoff and add a TTL or an external replay trigger.
